stories.headline: AI designs first custom miniproteins to switch GPCR drug targets on and off, in Nature

key_facts.fact: A study published May 21 in Nature by the UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design and Skape Bio shows for the first time that AI can design proteins to activate or block G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs), one of the most important and hardest-to-target classes of drug targets.
key_facts.excerpt: The UW Medicine Institute for Protein Design and Skape Bio led a new study showing for the first time that AI can be used to create computationally designed proteins to activate or block GPCRs. Their findings are published in Nature.

key_facts.fact: The team generated functional lead molecules - both agonists and antagonists - against 11 GPCR targets, including receptors implicated in cancer, diabetes, obesity, migraine, itch and pain.
key_facts.excerpt: the team generated agonists for receptors involved in itch and pain, and antagonists for receptors implicated in cancer, metabolic disease such as diabetes and obesity, and migraine.

key_facts.fact: Cryo-EM structures of five designed miniproteins closely matched their computational models, and in one mouse study a designed miniprotein performed comparably to a clinically used drug while showing fewer side effects.
key_facts.excerpt: Cryo-EM structures of five designed miniproteins closely matched their computational models, underscoring the accuracy of the design pipeline. In one mouse study, a [designed miniprotein performed] comparable to a [clinical drug].

key_facts.fact: The researchers also built a new high-throughput 'receptor diversion' screening system that can test up to 100,000 designs against full-length GPCRs in living human cells, keeping receptors in their native membrane environment.
key_facts.excerpt: a new high-throughput screening system that tests designed proteins against full-length GPCRs in living human cells. The system can evaluate up to 100,000 designs while keeping the receptors in their natural membrane environment.

stories.headline: EU to propose lifting China chip sanctions weeks after imposing them, to shield automakers

key_facts.fact: The European Commission will propose temporarily lifting sanctions on Chinese semiconductor supplier Yangzhou Yangjie Electronic Technology, possibly as early as this week.
key_facts.excerpt: The European Commission, the EU's executive arm, will propose the exemption for chip manufacturer Yangzhou Yangjie Electronic Technology as early as this week, according to people familiar with the matter.

key_facts.fact: Yangjie was added in April to the EU's 20th sanctions package targeting entities accused of supplying dual-use goods or weapons systems to Russia, with its products allegedly found in drones and glide bombs used against Ukraine.
key_facts.excerpt: Yangjie Electronic was included in the EU's 20th sanctions package... The Chinese semiconductor firm was sanctioned in April after dozens of shipments of its technologies allegedly reached Russia and its products were found in drones and glide bombs used against Ukraine.

key_facts.fact: European automakers lobbied to delay the ban, warning that chip inventories would be depleted within weeks and force production stoppages across the continent.
key_facts.excerpt: European automakers warned that without the derogation, chip inventories would be exhausted within weeks, forcing production stoppages across the continent.

key_facts.fact: Any derogation would be temporary, lasting several months to give industry time to find alternative suppliers, and would require approval from all 27 EU member states.
key_facts.excerpt: Any derogation would be temporary and likely last several months to give the industry more time to find alternative suppliers.

key_facts.fact: The move follows the Nexperia crisis, in which the Dutch government seized control of the chipmaker from Chinese parent Wingtech and Beijing retaliated with export controls, forcing temporary shutdowns at Honda, Volkswagen and Bosch.
key_facts.excerpt: Yangjie had become a crutch for sourcing components after the Dutch government seized control of Nexperia from its Chinese parent Wingtech last October. Beijing retaliated with export controls on the chipmaker's Chinese-made output, forcing temporary production shutdowns at Honda, Volkswagen, Bosch, and others.

stories.headline: FDA approves AstraZeneca's Baxfendy, a first-in-class drug for uncontrolled hypertension

key_facts.fact: The US FDA approved AstraZeneca's Baxfendy (baxdrostat), a first-in-class aldosterone synthase inhibitor, to treat hypertension in combination with other antihypertensives in adults whose blood pressure is not adequately controlled.
key_facts.excerpt: AstraZeneca's Baxfendy (baxdrostat) has been approved by the US FDA as a first-in-class aldosterone synthase inhibitor (ASI) to treat hypertension in combination with other antihypertensive medications, to lower blood pressure in adults who are not adequately controlled.

key_facts.fact: Approval was based on the Phase 3 BaxHTN trial, which showed statistically significant systolic blood pressure reductions at both 2mg and 1mg doses in patients with uncontrolled and resistant hypertension already on two or more medications.
key_facts.excerpt: The approval was based on positive results from the BaxHTN phase 3 trial, with Baxfendy demonstrating statistically significant and clinically meaningful seated systolic blood pressure reduction at both 2mg and 1mg doses in patients with uncontrolled and resistant hypertension on two or more medications.

key_facts.fact: Baxfendy was generally well-tolerated with no unanticipated safety findings; hypertension affects more than 1.4 billion people worldwide, many uncontrolled despite multiple therapies.
key_facts.excerpt: Baxfendy was generally well-tolerated with no unanticipated safety findings. Hypertension affects more than 1.4 billion people worldwide and many patients remain uncontrolled despite multiple therapies.

The executive order is the first of its kind signed by any U.S. official, and orders state agencies to collaborate with labor groups, academics and the AI industry.

key_facts.fact: The order directs agencies to study possible subsidies for companies that retain workers instead of replacing them with AI, along with expanded retraining (especially for customer-service, sales and software-development roles), revised severance standards and expanded unemployment insurance.

key_facts.fact: The more than dozen directives also include a study into universal basic income and 'universal basic capital' - giving every Californian a stake in assets such as corporate stocks, bonds and wealth funds.
key_facts.excerpt: a concept the governor called 'universal basic capital,' giving all residents a stake in assets such as corporate stocks, bonds or wealth funds.

key_facts.fact: The order follows a March 2026 Newsom order requiring vetting of AI companies that do business with the state, and may conflict with the Trump administration's hands-off approach and its push to preempt state AI rules.

stories.headline: Trump abruptly postpones AI executive order after last-minute tech-industry lobbying

key_facts.fact: Trump called off a Thursday (May 21) Oval Office ceremony to sign a new AI and cybersecurity executive order, saying he disliked the draft text: 'Because I didn't like certain aspects of it, I postponed it ... we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead.'
key_facts.excerpt: "Because I didn't like certain aspects of it, I postponed it," Mr. Trump said ... "I think it gets in the way of, you know, we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead."

key_facts.fact: The draft order would have tasked the Office of the National Cyber Director and other agencies with building a process to evaluate AI models for security before release; a key sticking point was a proposed voluntary framework asking AI developers to share 'covered frontier models' with the government between 14 and 90 days ahead of launch.
key_facts.excerpt: The anticipated executive order would have tasked the Office of the National Cyber Director and other agencies with developing a process to evaluate AI models for security before their release ... a proposed requirement for AI companies to share advanced models with the government between 14 and 90 days ahead of launch.

key_facts.fact: The push for pre-release vetting followed concern over the cyber capabilities of Anthropic's Mythos model and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber, both of which can quickly find and exploit software vulnerabilities.
key_facts.excerpt: This is partly in response to concerns from the release of Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber - both of which can quickly find and exploit security vulnerabilities.

key_facts.fact: Four sources told Politico the delay was due in part to leading tech executives being unable to attend on short notice; some CEOs had been invited and were reportedly already midair en route to Washington when the White House reversed course.
key_facts.excerpt: top tech executives had been invited to the signing ceremony - some were even midair, en route to Washington. Then, hours before the signing, the White House abruptly reversed course, postponing the executive order.

key_facts.fact: The Washington Post reported that last-minute calls from Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg and David Sacks helped persuade Trump not to sign, with Sacks telling the president that federal pre-release reviews would slow innovation and hurt the US in its AI race with China.
key_facts.excerpt: Industry leaders warned in last-minute calls to the president that the proposed safety vetting system could inhibit development of the pivotal technology.

stories.headline: Trump postpones AI security order signing, says it 'could have been a blocker'

key_facts.fact: The White House abruptly postponed the Thursday afternoon (May 21) ceremony for Trump to sign an executive order on AI and cybersecurity, hours before it was due.
key_facts.excerpt: The White House postponed a highly anticipated signing of an artificial intelligence executive order, according to four people with knowledge of the matter.

key_facts.fact: Trump said he postponed it because 'I didn't like certain aspects of it... we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead,' calling it a potential 'blocker.'
key_facts.excerpt: 'Because I didn't like certain aspects of it, I postponed it,' Mr. Trump said. 'I think it gets in the way of, you know, we're leading China, we're leading everybody, and I don't want to do anything that's going to get in the way of that lead.'

key_facts.fact: The order would have established a voluntary framework giving the federal government pre-release access to 'covered frontier models', with a proposed 90-day review window that some industry leaders wanted cut to 14 days.
key_facts.excerpt: One of the key sticking points in the EO's language, per CNN, is a proposed requirement for AI companies to share advanced models with the government between 14 and 90 days ahead of launch.

key_facts.fact: It would also have directed agencies to use advanced AI to strengthen cybersecurity for federal, state and local systems and critical sectors like banks and hospitals.
key_facts.excerpt: The executive order was intended to help protect US computer systems from powerful artificial intelligence that could give bad actors unprecedented powers.

key_facts.fact: Reports cite a more mundane reason: several tech CEOs invited to the photo op could not reach Washington on short notice, with some reportedly midair when the event was called off.
key_facts.excerpt: The unofficial reason: Not enough tech CEOs could make it to Washington, D.C. on short notice, according to several reports. And what's an executive order signing without a photo op?

key_facts.fact: The effort grew from cyber-risk fears tied to powerful models like Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber, which can quickly find and exploit security vulnerabilities.
key_facts.excerpt: This is partly in response to concerns from the release of Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's GPT-5.5 Cyber, both of which can quickly find and exploit security vulnerabilities.

stories.headline: Broadcom, Meta, Applied Materials, GlobalFoundries, Synopsys launch $125M UCLA chip hub

key_facts.fact: Broadcom, Applied Materials, GlobalFoundries, Meta and Synopsys are founding partners of a new $125 million Semiconductor Hub at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering.
key_facts.excerpt: Founding partners behind the $125 million effort include Broadcom, Applied Materials, GlobalFoundries, Meta and Synopsys.

key_facts.fact: The hub focuses on energy-efficient, AI-powered chip technologies and spans chip design, software, manufacturing, equipment and advanced materials, starting with an initial five-year commitment.
key_facts.excerpt: The initial five-year commitment will establish a long-term collaboration across the semiconductor ecosystem, spanning chip design, software, manufacturing, equipment and advanced materials.

key_facts.fact: The effort is pitched as strengthening US leadership and workforce development in chip technologies critical to economic growth and national security, with faculty and student researchers working alongside the founding companies to shorten innovation timelines.
key_facts.excerpt: A first-of-its-kind Semiconductor Hub at the UCLA Samueli School of Engineering aims to accelerate research, strengthen U.S. leadership and support workforce development in energy-efficient AI-powered chip technologies critical to economic growth and national security.

stories.headline: US Commerce to put $2B into nine quantum firms via CHIPS Act, taking equity stakes

key_facts.fact: The US Department of Commerce signed letters of intent to provide $2.013 billion in CHIPS and Science Act incentives to nine quantum companies, and will take a minority, non-controlling equity stake in each as a condition of the funding.
key_facts.excerpt: The Department of Commerce today announced the signing of 9 letters of intent to provide $2.013 billion in federal incentives under the CHIPS and Science Act... The Department will receive a minority, non-controlling equity stake in each company as a condition for receiving the funds.

key_facts.fact: Two of the nine are designated 'quantum foundry' companies: IBM gets $1 billion to set up a new standalone subsidiary called Anderon in New Albany, New York to manufacture quantum-grade superconducting wafers, and GlobalFoundries gets $375 million for a domestic quantum foundry.
key_facts.excerpt: The most substantial funding is slated for the two foundry companies, with $375 million for Global Foundries and $1 billion for IBM... 'will operate as a state-of-the-art 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry.'

key_facts.fact: The seven quantum-computing recipients are Atom Computing, Diraq, D-Wave, Infleqtion, PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Rigetti; Diraq receives $38 million and the other six get about $100 million each.
key_facts.excerpt: $2.013 billion in CHIPS funding will go to IBM, GlobalFoundries, Atom Computing, Diraq, D-Wave, Infleqtion, PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Rigetti... Diraq, which specializes in quantum computing via silicon spin qubits, received $38 million. The other six each received $100 million.

key_facts.fact: IBM said it would itself contribute an additional $1 billion to Anderon, calling it 'America's first pure-play quantum foundry'; GlobalFoundries said Commerce's stake represents roughly 1% ownership.
key_facts.excerpt: A $1 billion 'incentive' from the Department of Commerce would support the research and development efforts of a new IBM company called Anderon, 'America's first pure-play quantum foundry'... IBM said it would invest an addition $1 billion into Anderon.

key_facts.fact: Quantum stocks jumped on the news, with D-Wave and Rigetti shares gaining about 14% and 12% respectively and IBM rising nearly 4% at the open.
key_facts.excerpt: smaller firms such as D-Wave Quantum and Rigetti Computing, which are both due to receive up to $100 million in exchange for equity... The companies' shares gained 14% and 12% respectively... Its shares gained nearly 4% at the open.

stories.headline: US Commerce awards $2B to nine quantum firms and takes equity stakes; IBM gets $1B

key_facts.fact: The US Department of Commerce signed letters of intent on May 21 to provide $2.013 billion in CHIPS and Science Act incentives to nine quantum companies.
key_facts.excerpt: The Department of Commerce today announced the signing of 9 letters of intent to provide $2.013 billion in federal incentives under the CHIPS and Science Act.

key_facts.fact: Funding goes to two 'quantum foundry' companies, GlobalFoundries ($375M) and IBM ($1B), plus seven quantum computing firms: Atom Computing, Diraq, D-Wave, Infleqtion, PsiQuantum, Quantinuum and Rigetti.
key_facts.excerpt: The most substantial funding is slated for the two foundry companies, with $375 million for Global Foundries and $1 billion for IBM. The other companies received between $38 and $100 million each.

key_facts.fact: D-Wave, Rigetti and Infleqtion will each get about $100 million, while Diraq will receive up to $38 million.
key_facts.excerpt: Other firms including D-Wave, Rigetti Computing and Infleqtion will get about $100 million each, while Diraq will receive up to $38 million.

key_facts.fact: The Department of Commerce will receive a minority, non-controlling equity stake in each company as a condition for the funds, to 'enhance the return for the U.S. taxpayer.'
key_facts.excerpt: The Department will receive a minority, non-controlling equity stake in each company as a condition for receiving the funds to enhance the return for the U.S. taxpayer.

key_facts.fact: IBM's $1 billion will fund a new standalone company called Anderon, based in New Albany, New York, billed as America's first dedicated quantum chip manufacturing facility.
key_facts.excerpt: IBM announced the CHIPS incentive would support research-and-development efforts of a new company called Anderon. That standalone IBM company 'will operate as a state-of-the-art 300-millimeter quantum wafer foundry.'

key_facts.fact: The Trump administration framed the move as a push to secure US leadership in quantum and counter China.
key_facts.excerpt: The Trump administration will take $2 billion in equity stakes across nine quantum-computing companies, including a new IBM venture, in a major push to secure U.S. leadership in the emerging technology and counter China.
